lessons.title: Ante-mortem inspection of cattle
lessons.html:
Inspecting cattle in the lairage

Cattle arrive at the abattoir by truck from farms, feedlots and auctions. Before slaughter, every animal must be inspected in the lairage under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000. Look at the group first, then at individual animals, at rest and while they walk.

What to look for

  • Movement: lameness, swollen joints, animals that cannot rise (downer animals).
  • Breathing: coughing, fast or laboured breathing, frothing at the mouth.
  • Mouth, nose and feet: blisters, drooling or lameness may point to foot-and-mouth disease, which is notifiable.
  • Skin and body: lumps, abscesses, ringworm, heavy tick burden, wounds and bruises.
  • Condition: very thin animals, swollen bellies (bloat), signs of fever.
  • Identification: brand marks, ear tags and the movement documents that came with the animals.

Decisions

Normal animals go forward for slaughter. Suspect animals are marked and kept in a separate pen for the veterinarian. Animals that are injured or in pain must be slaughtered first or handled under the veterinarian's instruction so they do not suffer. Animals showing signs of a notifiable disease must be isolated and reported immediately; do not let them be slaughtered until the veterinarian decides.

Handling and welfare

Watch how workers move the cattle. Electric prodders must only be used as allowed by the abattoir's procedures, never on the face, eyes or genitals. Beating and twisting tails are offences under the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962. Cattle must have water in the lairage. Rough handling causes bruising, which you will later have to trim off the carcass.

Your safety

Cattle can kick and crush. Stay on walkways or behind barriers, never enter a pen alone with a stressed bull, and always have an escape route.

lessons.title: Inspecting the beef head and offal
lessons.html:
The head

The head is removed, washed and identified with the carcass. Inspect it on the head rack or hook.

  • View the outer surfaces, mouth, lips and tongue for blisters, wounds and lumps.
  • Incise the lymph nodes of the head (submandibular, parotid and retropharyngeal) and look for abscesses, caseous (cheese-like) or calcified lesions that may indicate tuberculosis.
  • Incise the cheek (masseter) muscles and examine the tongue to look for beef measles (Cysticercus bovis), the cyst stage of the human tapeworm Taenia saginata.

The red offal

Lungs

View and palpate both lungs. Incise the bronchial and mediastinal lymph nodes. Look for pneumonia, abscesses, tuberculosis lesions and hydatid cysts. Lungs with aspirated blood or scald water are condemned.

Heart

View the outer surface, open the heart and incise the muscle to look for measles cysts. Look for inflammation of the heart lining or sac.

Liver

View and palpate. Incise the bile ducts on the underside to check for liver fluke. Look for abscesses, hydatid cysts and telangiectasis (dark blood spots). Fluke-damaged livers are usually condemned, but the carcass can pass if it is otherwise healthy.

Kidneys and spleen

Kidneys are usually inspected in the carcass after removing the fat. Look for cysts, stones or discolouration. View the spleen for swelling; a very large, dark spleen with dark, tarry blood can be a sign of anthrax. If anthrax is suspected, stop, do not cut further, isolate the carcass and call the veterinarian immediately.

The green offal

View the stomachs and intestines for inflammation, abscesses and contamination, and check the mesenteric lymph nodes. Rumen content spilled on the carcass is a contamination defect and must be trimmed.

lessons.title: Carcass inspection and judgement
lessons.html:
Inspecting the beef carcass

Inspect both sides of the split carcass, outside and inside. Work from top to bottom so nothing is missed.

  • Outer surfaces: bruises, abscesses, injection site lesions, hair, dung and other contamination.
  • Inner surfaces: pleura (chest lining) and peritoneum (belly lining) for inflammation, adhesions and tuberculosis lesions.
  • Lymph nodes: view or incise the carcass lymph nodes as required by your procedures, for example the prescapular and superficial inguinal nodes.
  • Muscles: check colour and look at cut surfaces for measles cysts and blood splash.
  • Bleeding and colour: a poorly bled, dark or yellow carcass can point to fever or jaundice.
  • Smell: abnormal smells such as urine or medicine.

Judgement

FindingUsual action
Small bruise or local abscessTrim the affected part and pass
Fluke in liver onlyCondemn liver, pass carcass
Measles cysts foundDetain for the veterinarian; judgement depends on how many cysts are found, following the regulations
Generalised tuberculosis, fever or jaundiceDetain; usually total condemnation
Faecal contaminationTrim; do not wash it off

When in doubt, detain. A detained carcass goes to the detention rail with its head and offal, and the veterinarian makes the final decision.

Marking and recording

Passed carcasses receive the approved stamp. Write down every condemnation, the reason and the owner, and report notifiable conditions to the state veterinarian.

Key points

  • Inspect cattle at rest and in motion in the lairage; isolate suspected notifiable disease.
  • Incise the head lymph nodes and cheek muscles; check the tongue and heart for beef measles.
  • Incise the liver bile ducts for fluke and palpate the lungs.
  • Suspected anthrax: do not cut, isolate and call the veterinarian.
  • Trim faecal contamination; never wash it off.
  • When in doubt, detain the carcass with its head and offal.
